This question probes cross-device AR synchronization, offline resilience, and conflict resolution—skills valuable for real-world AR apps at scale.

## Key Concepts

- ARKit anchors, world tracking, anchor fusion
- CloudKit/REST sync, version vectors, CRDT-like merges
- Offline-first design, conflict resolution UX
- Testing: drift, race conditions, reconciliation

## Code Example

```swift
struct AnchorRecord: Codable {
  let id: String
  var posX: Float; var posY: Float; var posZ: Float
  var rotX: Float; var rotY: Float; var rotZ: Float; var rotW: Float
  var version: Int
}
func merge(remote: AnchorRecord, local: inout AnchorRecord) {
  if remote.version > local.version {
    local = remote
  }
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you detect and resolve anchor drift during long AR sessions?
- What backend schema supports millions of anchors across devices?

questions.explanation:
## Memory Management

Swift uses ARC (Automatic Reference Counting) to manage memory automatically. Strong references can create retain cycles, so we use weak and unowned references to break them.

## Weak References

- Always optional (automatically set to nil on deallocation)
- Use for optional relationships
- Common patterns: delegates, outlets

```swift
weak var delegate: MyDelegate?
```

## Unowned References

- Non-optional (assumes reference always exists)
- Use when you know the reference will outlive the holder
- Common patterns: parent-child relationships

```swift
unowned let parent: ParentClass
```

## Key Differences

Choose weak when the reference might become nil during execution. Choose unowned when you're certain the reference will always exist throughout the object's lifetime.
